book.title: The Campaign in Tirah, 1897–1898
book.subtitle: An Account of the Expedition against the Orakzais and Afridis under General Sir William Lockhart
book.author: henry-doveton-hutchinson

description.short: One of the great contemporary military narratives of the Victorian North-West Frontier.
description.long:
One of the great contemporary military narratives of the Victorian North-West Frontier.

In 1897 a major rising spread across India’s frontier. Afridi and Orakzai fighters seized positions in the Khyber and challenged British authority throughout the mountain districts.

The answer was the Tirah Expeditionary Force under General Sir William S. A. Lockhart: more than thirty thousand British and Indian troops supported by cavalry, mountain artillery, Gurkhas, Sikh regiments, Punjabi infantry, pioneers, engineers, hospitals and an immense transport organisation.

Their campaign produced one of the most celebrated infantry actions of the Victorian Army—the storming of the Dargai Heights—but Tirah was far more than Dargai. Hutchinson follows the forcing of the mountain passes, operations in the Maidan and Mastura valleys, convoy and rear-guard fighting, severe winter marches and the tactical and logistical problems of keeping a large army alive in hostile high country.

At Dargai alone four Victoria Crosses were won.

Originally written from Hutchinson’s contemporary letters to The Times, the book was praised by Nature for the author’s unusual ability to extract professional military lessons from the campaign. Hutchinson was not merely an observer: he was an Indian Army officer and Director of Military Education in India.

author_page.name: Henry Doveton Hutchinson
kopfzeilen: Companion of the Order of the Star of India
Born 13 September 1847 · baptised at Dinapore, Bengal
text_absaetze: Henry Doveton Hutchinson belonged to a generation for whom soldiering and the professional study of soldiering were not separate occupations.

Born on 13 September 1847, he entered the Indian military service and developed a career that combined regimental duty, active operations, military education and writing. He served in the Sikkim operations of 1887–88, during the Relief of Chitral in 1895 and in the Tirah campaign of 1897–98. He raised the 2nd Battalion, 3rd Gurkha Rifles in 1891 and later commanded troops in Chitral. From 1896 to 1901 he served as Director of Military Education in India. His later career included duty at the India Office, appointment as Assistant Military Secretary for Indian affairs and service as Director of Staff Duties at the War Office. He eventually retired as a Lieutenant-General and was appointed Companion of the Order of the Star of India.
At the time The Campaign in Tirah appeared in 1898, Hutchinson was a Colonel.

That contemporary rank matters because the book belongs to the middle of his professional life rather than its retrospective end. He was writing not as an elderly memoirist recalling a vanished army, but as an officer still actively engaged in the business of military education.

His bibliography reveals the range of that interest. He wrote upon military sketching, field fortification, Waterloo, Corunna and other campaigns, and later produced regimental history. His concern was consistently practical: how armies understood ground, how men were instructed, how tactical lessons were extracted from experience and how military knowledge might be transmitted before another campaign forced the same lessons to be purchased again.
The Tirah volume occupies a special position within that work.

Hutchinson had contributed letters to The Times while impressions remained fresh and then enlarged the material for book publication with subsequent information. He deliberately avoided converting his introduction into a partisan treatise on frontier policy; instead he sought to provide the general reader sufficient facts to understand the origin of the conflict and then concentrated upon the conduct of the campaign itself.
That professional restraint remains one of the strengths of the book.
Hutchinson is interested in bravery, but also in why an attack succeeded.
He is interested in a regiment, but also in what stood beside it.
He sees a pass as terrain rather than scenery.
He treats transport as a fighting necessity.
The result is a campaign history written by an officer who believed that military experience was wasted unless somebody learned from it.
By then the Army he had known had passed through the South African War and the immense transformation of 1914–18.
The lesson beneath his work nevertheless remained intact:
an army that does not study yesterday may be forced to learn it again tomorrow.
